threads.title: I built YouTubeRAG because n8n kept failing
tweets:
I built YouTubeRAG because n8n kept failing me.

90 minutes to build. Infinitely more reliable.

Here's how it works (and how you can build one too):

1/ The Problem

n8n + RapidAPI workflow for YouTube transcripts.

Broke constantly. Rate limits. API changes. Random failures.

I was spending more time fixing automation than it saved.

2/ The Solution: Build My Own

FastAPI microservice on port 3011.

Components:
• youtube-transcript-api for extraction
• SpaCy for semantic chunking
• OpenAI for embeddings
• ChromaDB for vector storage

3/ The Pipeline

Input: YouTube video/playlist URL

1. Extract transcripts
2. Chunk into semantic segments
3. Generate embeddings
4. Store in vector DB
5. Ready for queries

17 videos → 103 chunks → searchable knowledge base.

4/ The Chunking Strategy

Not fixed-size. Semantic.

Using SpaCy to detect topic boundaries.
Preserving time markers for navigation.

Result: Chunks that make sense, not arbitrary splits.

5/ The Query Interface

Natural language in → relevant chunks out.

"What's the best scraping technique?"
→ Top 3 relevant segments
→ Source video + timestamp
→ Full context preserved

6/ The Architecture Win

Made it an API. Not siloed to one project.

Now ANY project can:
• Ingest videos
• Query the knowledge base
• Get cited answers

Infrastructure that compounds.

7/ Time Comparison

Manual note-taking: 40 minutes per video
YouTubeRAG query: 30 seconds

Built once. Use forever.

That's the power of owning your automation.

threads.title: Most people use Claude Code wrong
tweets:
Most people use Claude Code wrong.

They treat it like a chatbot.

Here's how to treat it like an agentic coding partner (thread):

1/ The Mindset Shift

Chatbot: Ask question → get answer
Agent: Describe goal → watch it work

Claude Code can read files, run commands, make changes.

Let it.

2/ Context is Everything

Claude's context window fills fast.

Every file read, every command output = tokens consumed.

Manage context like a precious resource.

/clear between unrelated tasks. Always.

3/ Skills > Prompts

Prompts are one-time.
Skills persist.

I have 24 reusable skills:
• Code review patterns
• Debug workflows
• Content frameworks

One file = consistent results every session.

4/ Let Claude Verify Itself

Don't just accept output.

Give Claude ways to check its work:
• Run the tests
• Check the types
• Compare screenshots

Verification is the highest-leverage thing you can do.

5/ Use Subagents for Exploration

Don't pollute your main context with investigation.

"Use a subagent to explore how auth works"

Subagent explores. Reports back. Your context stays clean.

6/ The Anti-Patterns

• Kitchen sink sessions (mixing unrelated tasks)
• Correction loops (fix → wrong → fix → wrong)
• Over-specified CLAUDE.md (too long = ignored)

Recognize them. Avoid them.

7/ The Result

Claude goes from "helpful assistant" to "autonomous coding partner."

It explores. It plans. It implements. It verifies.

You watch, redirect, or step away entirely.

threads.title: Your RAG system is probably broken
tweets:
Your RAG system is probably broken.

And you don't know it because you're not measuring the right things.

Here's what I learned building YouTubeRAG (thread):

1/ The Common Mistakes

• Fixed-size chunks (breaks mid-thought)
• Pure vector search (misses exact matches)
• No source attribution (can't verify)
• Giant context windows (slow, expensive)

Most RAG tutorials teach these.

2/ Chunking Strategy Matters

Don't split on character count.

Use semantic boundaries:
• Topic changes
• Speaker transitions
• Natural pauses

SpaCy can detect these automatically.

3/ Hybrid Search Wins

Vector search: "What's the concept?"
Keyword search: "Where's the exact term?"

Use both.

My YouTubeRAG combines semantic + keyword.
Retrieval quality: dramatically better.

4/ Metadata is Crucial

Store with each chunk:
• Source document
• Timestamp/position
• Original context
• Confidence score

You'll need these for verification and navigation.

5/ Context Window Management

Don't stuff everything in.

Retrieve relevant chunks → rerank → take top K.

Less context = faster, cheaper, often more accurate.

6/ Test Your Retrieval

Before connecting to an LLM:
• Query the vector DB directly
• Check if right chunks return
• Measure precision/recall

Bad retrieval + good LLM = garbage output.

7/ The Meta-Lesson

RAG isn't about the model.

It's about:
• How you chunk
• How you embed
• How you retrieve

Fix the pipeline. Then worry about the model.

A special file Claude reads at the start of every session.

New project inherits from parent.

• ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (global defaults)
• /project/CLAUDE.md (project-specific)
• /project/subdir/CLAUDE.md (area-specific)

Claude reads all that apply. More specific wins.

6/ Emphasis Tricks

"IMPORTANT: Always run tests before committing"
"YOU MUST use TypeScript strict mode"

Emphasis improves adherence.

Claude pays attention to strong language.

7/ The Result

Before: Re-explain project every session.
After: Claude knows everything automatically.

Context that persists = compounding productivity.

That's the power of CLAUDE.md.

threads.title: How I debug automation failures systematically
tweets:
How I debug automation failures systematically.

My scheduler broke for 3 days. Here's how I fixed it (thread):

1/ The Symptom

60 agents weren't running.
No errors in logs.
Scheduler started fine.

Silent failure. The worst kind.

2/ Step 1: Verify the Basics

• Is the script executable?
• Are paths correct?
• Are dependencies installed?
• Are env vars set?

Often the fix is embarrassingly simple.

3/ Step 2: Trace the Execution

Add logging at every step:
• Script started
• Each agent triggered
• Each agent completed
• Errors caught

Find where execution stops.

4/ Step 3: Check Environment

Cron/LaunchAgent run in different env than terminal.

• Different PATH
• Different working directory
• Different permissions

Print env vars. Compare to manual run.

5/ The Root Cause

Hardcoded path: /Users/old/path/to/project

Worked until I moved folders.

Scheduler tried to access non-existent path.
Failed silently because of error handling.

Lesson: Never hardcode paths.

6/ The Fix

• Use relative paths
• Use environment variables
• Make error handling loud, not quiet
• Add health checks that alert on failure

7/ The Prevention

Now every agent has:
• Verbose logging option
• Health check endpoint
• Failure alerts
• Self-healing restart logic

Silent failures are now impossible.

4/ Framework 3: How-To

"How I [achieve result]:"

"How [action] to [outcome]:"

threads.title: Simple automation beats complex automation
tweets:
Simple automation beats complex automation.

Every time.

Here's what I learned building 60+ agents (thread):

1/ The Temptation

Build one mega-script that:
• Handles all cases
• Has every feature
• Covers every edge case

Feels comprehensive.
Actually fragile.

2/ The Reality

Complex automation:
• Hard to debug
• Hard to modify
• Fails catastrophically
• Single point of failure

Simple automation:
• Easy to understand
• Easy to fix
• Fails gracefully
• Isolated failures

3/ My Rule

One agent = one job.

Not "project management agent."

Instead:
• GitHub sync agent
• TODO aggregation agent
• Security scoring agent

Composable pieces.

4/ The Coordination Layer

Daily scheduler orchestrates.
Agents do the work.

Scheduler is simple: call agents in sequence.
Agents are simple: do one thing well.

Complexity in coordination, not execution.

5/ Error Handling Philosophy

Old: Catch everything, never fail.
New: Fail fast, log loudly, alert me.

I'd rather know about problems than have them hidden.

6/ The Maintenance Burden

Complex: Hours to understand, minutes to break.
Simple: Minutes to understand, seconds to fix.

Your future self will thank you.

7/ The Meta-Lesson

Automation should reduce complexity, not add it.

If your automation needs automation, you've gone too far.

Simple. Reliable. Boring.

That's the goal.

threads.title: How I use Plan Mode effectively
tweets:
How I use Plan Mode effectively in Claude Code.

Explore first, then execute (thread):

1/ What is Plan Mode?

Claude explores without changing anything.
Reads files. Answers questions. Doesn't modify.

Safe exploration before risky execution.

2/ When to Use It

• Unfamiliar codebase
• Multiple approaches possible
• Changes affect many files
• Need to understand before acting

Complex tasks need exploration.

3/ The Workflow

Phase 1 - Explore:
"Read src/auth and explain how sessions work."

Phase 2 - Plan:
"I want to add OAuth. What files need to change?"

Phase 3 - Implement:
[Exit Plan Mode] "Implement the OAuth flow."

4/ What to Ask in Explore

• How does X work?
• Where is Y implemented?
• What patterns does this codebase use?
• What would break if I changed Z?

Understanding before action.

5/ What to Ask in Plan

• What files need to change?
• What's the sequence of changes?
• What tests should I write?
• What could go wrong?

Map before you move.

6/ When NOT to Use It

• Simple, obvious tasks
• You know the codebase well
• Change is isolated to one file
• Time-sensitive fix

Planning adds overhead. Skip for trivial work.

7/ The Result

Fewer mistakes.
Better implementations.
Less wasted effort.

Explore → Plan → Execute.

That's how complex changes become manageable.

threads.title: How I manage context in long Claude Code sessions
tweets:
How I manage context in long Claude Code sessions.

The #1 resource to protect (thread):

1/ The Problem

Claude's context window fills fast:
• Every file read = tokens
• Every command output = tokens
• Every conversation turn = tokens

Full context = degraded performance.

2/ The Symptoms

• Claude "forgets" instructions
• Responses get confused
• Same mistakes repeated
• Quality drops noticeably

Context pollution is subtle. Then sudden.

3/ Strategy 1: /clear Between Tasks

Finished feature A?
/clear
Start feature B.

Fresh context = better performance.

Don't let unrelated tasks accumulate.

4/ Strategy 2: Use Subagents for Exploration

"Use a subagent to investigate the auth system."

Subagent explores in separate context.
Reports back summary.
Your context stays clean.

5/ Strategy 3: /compact When Needed

Need to preserve some context?
/compact Focus on the API changes

Claude summarizes, keeps what matters, frees space.

6/ Strategy 4: Stop Correction Loops

Claude wrong → correct → still wrong → correct again.

AFTER 2 CORRECTIONS:
/clear
Write a better initial prompt.

Fresh start > accumulated failures.

7/ The Rule of Thumb

• One major task per session
• Clear between unrelated tasks
• Subagents for exploration
• Stop correction loops early

Context management = productivity management.

threads.title: How I handle failure publicly
tweets:
How I handle failure publicly.

Failures teach more than successes (thread):

1/ The Default Response

Something breaks.
Hide it.
Fix it quietly.
Never mention it.

Protect the image.

But this misses the opportunity.

2/ The Better Response

Something breaks.
Document it.
Share the root cause.
Explain the fix.

Turn failure into content.

3/ Why It Works

• Relatable (everyone fails)
• Educational (how to fix)
• Authentic (not just highlight reel)
• Memorable (stories > tips)

Vulnerability creates connection.

4/ Example: Scheduler Failure

My 60-agent system broke for 3 days.

Shared:
• What happened (hardcoded path)
• How I found it (added logging)
• How I fixed it (environment variables)
• How I prevented it (health checks)

Thread got 5x normal engagement.

5/ The Framework

1. What broke?
2. What was the symptom?
3. What was the root cause?
4. How did you fix it?
5. How do you prevent it?

Structure for failure stories.

6/ What NOT to Share

• Security vulnerabilities (fix first)
• Customer data issues (privacy)
• Legal problems (get advice first)
• Ongoing incidents (after resolution)

Transparency has limits.

7/ The Mindset

Every failure = content opportunity.

You're going to fail anyway.
Might as well extract value from it.

Failure → Learning → Sharing → Growth.

Every post:

• Wildly varying quality
• No predictable results

Creative chaos.

2/ The Insight

Viral content follows patterns.

Patterns can be codified.

Codeified patterns = frameworks.

Frameworks = repeatable results.

3/ Framework 1: Hook Types

• Contrarian: Challenge beliefs
• Transformation: Before/after
• How-To: Step-by-step
• Benefit-Driven: Clear value

Every post fits one type.

4/ Framework 2: Power Words

Words that trigger engagement:

• "Why most people..."
• "The exact process..."
• "How I 10x'd..."
• "What nobody tells you..."

Psychological triggers.

5/ Framework 3: Structure

Every post has:
• Hook (first line)
• Body (the meat)
• CTA (what to do next)

No mystery. Just fill the template.

6/ Framework 4: Quality Score

Before posting, score:
• Hook strength (1-10)
• Specificity (1-10)
• Value delivered (1-10)
• Platform fit (1-10)

Below 8 average? Don't post.

7/ The Result

Content quality scores: 60 → 85.
Engagement: more consistent.
Creation time: faster.
Creative energy: preserved.

Frameworks free creativity. They don't constrain it.

threads.title: How I pick which projects to share
tweets:
How I pick which projects to share.

Not everything is content-worthy (thread):

1/ The Filter

Not every project should be public.

Some are:
• Too niche
• Too boring
• Too personal
• Not ready

Curation matters.

2/ Criterion 1: Relatability

Will others have this problem?

Vendor quotes → common pain
Personal journaling app → too niche

Share problems others have.

3/ Criterion 2: Teachability

Can I explain how I built it?

Clear architecture → good content
Spaghetti code → not yet

Share when you can teach.

4/ Criterion 3: Completeness

Is there a story arc?

Problem → Solution → Results
Not just "started a project."

Share complete journeys.

5/ Criterion 4: Authenticity

Did I actually use this?
Does it solve a real problem?

Dogfooded projects > toy projects.

Share real usage.

6/ The 40 Projects Filter

40 active projects.
~15 are content-worthy.
~25 are too niche or incomplete.

Quality over quantity.

Share the best, not everything.

7/ The Meta-Rule

Ask: "Would I click on this if someone else posted it?"

No? Don't post.
Yes? Develop the content.

Self-filter before you publish.
